verses.note: The ruler's reign brings an abundance that reverses the curse on the ground (3:17-19). The prophets use the same picture of overflowing wine for the age of restoration (Amos 9:13, Joel 3:18).

Whatever the riddle means, the frame is clear: God will ‘create’ something new, using the verb of Genesis 1. Restoration is presented as an act of creation, not merely repair. Isaiah 43:19 and 65:17 speak the same way, and the New Testament takes up the idea in Paul's ‘new creation’ (2 Corinthians 5:17).

The language of Genesis 1:28 marks restoration as a new beginning. The book's hope is not only return but creation renewed, a theme that climaxes in the Eden picture of verse 35 and in the river of chapter 47.

Eden is the Bible's picture of the world as God meant it, with God and people together. Isaiah 51:3 promises the same for Zion. The hope of a restored Eden runs through Ezekiel's temple river (47:1-12) to Revelation's tree of life (Revelation 22:1-2).
